episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Stewart
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Charles Stewart was the hanging of a Black man accused of murdering his wife, whom a mob took from the county jail at Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, about midnight on Monday, August 15, 1881. The local paper reported that the crowd demanding his death was made up of Black men and women, and a widely reprinted wire item said his father-in-law prayed for him and then helped hang him. The nearest newspaper condemned the lynching because Stewart had been awaiting trial in circuit court on circumstantial evidence.

episodes.title: Killing of a Black prisoner near Horn Lake, Mississippi
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The killing of a Black prisoner near Horn Lake, Mississippi, took place in late August 1881, when four or five armed men stopped a marshal taking an unnamed Black man to jail at Hernando, ordered the marshal away and shot the prisoner dead on the road. The Memphis Daily Appeal reported it as a murder, and no arrests were reported.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Epperson
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of William Epperson took place on August 13, 1881, near Abbeville in Vermilion Parish, Louisiana, when a crowd took him from the parish jail and hanged him. Epperson, a Black man, had been arrested that morning on the accusation that he murdered the wife and daughter of Pine Henderson, a Black resident of the parish. The local paper and the Baton Rouge press described the crowd as made up of both white and Black men and presented the hanging as deserved punishment.

episodes.title: Orange, Texas, lynchings of 1881
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The Orange, Texas, lynchings of 1881 were the killings of several Black men by armed white citizens of Orange, Texas, on August 17-21, 1881, after Sheriff George W. Michael was shot pursuing Sam Saxon and others. Robert Saxon was hanged from an oak in town, others were shot, and on August 21 an armed party took Sam Saxon and another prisoner from the jail and shot them. Reported deaths ranged from three to eight, and the killings drew national wire coverage and a protest by Black residents of Galveston.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sam Saxon
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Sam Saxon took place on the night of Sunday, August 21, 1881, when an armed party of citizens took Saxon and a second Black prisoner from the jail at Orange, Texas, and shot them both dead. Saxon had surrendered that morning, accused of drawing Sheriff George Michael into an ambush four days earlier, after which his brother Robert had been hanged and other Black men shot. The killings drew national coverage and a Black protest meeting in Galveston.

episodes.title: Hanging of a Black man in Helton Township, Ashe County
episodes.doubt: single border-news letter (Western Sentinel 1881-08-25); 'a man by the name of Lynch' performed the hanging (a pun?); lawful or not unstated; 'not long since'
episodes.summary: The hanging of a Black man in Helton Township, Ashe County, was the killing of an unnamed Black man described as a "little negro dwarf" in northwestern North Carolina, reported in August 1881 as having taken place "not long since." He was hanged for allegedly stabbing a white girl, and the only report named the man who carried out the hanging as "a man by the name of Lynch."

episodes.title: Killing of Charles Dew
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The killing of Charles Dew was the murder of a Black farmer in Riley Township, Clinton County, Michigan, who was found beaten and hanged in his barn after the night of August 23, 1881. Weeks or months earlier a party of men had tarred and feathered him and threatened his life, and the killers were never identified in the coverage. Several Eastern papers carried the story under headlines calling it the work of Michigan "Kuklux".

episodes.title: Lynching of the "Black Kid" in Silverton, Colorado
episodes.doubt: lead from the MWT recall miss; the round never caught it; race from MWT
episodes.summary: The lynching of the "Black Kid" was the hanging of a young Black man by the Vigilance Committee of Silverton, Colorado, in late August 1881, after he was jailed in connection with the killing of the town's city marshal. Colorado papers called him the "Black Kid," while a Chicago Tribune correspondent named him Jim Catrin. Wire reports mentioned his death in a single sentence within the pursuit of the marshal's accused killers, one of whom, Burt Wilkinson, was later taken from the same jail and hanged.

episodes.title: Clubbing of Tom Wilson
episodes.summary: The clubbing of Tom Wilson was a police beating in Wadesboro, North Carolina, in about early August 1881, when two town policemen knocked Wilson, a Black man, senseless with their clubs while arresting him. A crowd of Black residents then rushed the officers, and the sheriff, the town marshal and a judge intervened; the only surviving report presented the affair as an "ugly sequel" to a political speech.

episodes.title: Lynching of Mike Wells
episodes.summary: The lynching of Mike Wells was the hanging of a Black man by a mob in the Court House yard at Dyersburg, Dyer County, Tennessee, on August 1, 1881. Wells had been arrested on an accusation of attempting to outrage a widow, Mrs. Childs, and was said to have confessed before the mob took him from his guard. The wire report ran in papers across the country, and later that month Governor Hawkins offered a $5,000 reward for the conviction of the men who had mobbed him.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Frank Hudson
episodes.doubt: threats at Albany Aug 18-20; seizure at Dawson about Aug 20-24
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Frank Hudson took place in southwest Georgia in August 1881, when crowds sought to kill Hudson, a Black man accused of an axe murder in Terrell County, first at the jail in Albany and then at Dawson. At Dawson a crowd of 1,500 to 2,000 people took him to the court house intending to execute him, but local citizens persuaded it to let him be jailed. Hudson was later convicted and sentenced to hang, after a Chicago paper had reported that he had probably been lynched.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Fred Henderson
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Fred Henderson took place at Canton, Kansas, in August 1881, when a mob clamored to lynch Henderson, a Black man charged with attempted rape. Henderson was acquitted at his preliminary hearing and returned to Emporia, and the Emporia weekly news, which had first reported the charge as his offense, declared him innocent.

episodes.title: Crisfield riot (1881)
episodes.summary: The Crisfield riot was an outbreak of violence in Crisfield, Maryland, on August 19 and 20, 1881, in which white men beat a Black man named Tucker, a white man named George Holland was shot in Goodsell's Alley, and a white crowd the next night took over the alley and fired on its Black residents. An elderly Black man was wounded and no arrests were reported, though a reward of up to $500 was later offered. Accounts in the Snow Hill and Baltimore papers differed over how the shooting began.

episodes.title: Lynching of Ed Reeves
episodes.summary: The lynching of Ed Reeves was the killing of a Black man by a mob in Ballard County, Kentucky, in mid-August 1881, after he was accused of an attempted assault on a woman in Graves County. Captured in Ballard County, he was taken from the men bringing him to the Graves County jail and, by most accounts, hanged. The story reached papers from Pennsylvania to Georgia as a short wire item, headed in some of them 'A BRUTE LYNCHED'.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Ed Anderson
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Ed Anderson took place near Oakley and Madisonville, outside Cincinnati, Ohio, in August 1881, when residents hunting two Black men accused of highway robbery caught Anderson and nearly lynched him. His companion escaped after about a hundred shots were fired at him, and Anderson was held as a prisoner. The capture ran as a wire item from Utah to Arizona, while only an Ohio weekly reported the near-lynching.

episodes.title: Lynching of Alex Wilson and Perry Munson
episodes.summary: The lynching of Alex Wilson and Perry Munson took place at Monroe, Louisiana, on the night of August 22-23, 1881, when a mob took the two Black prisoners from the parish jail and hanged them outside town. Both men were held on charges of murdering other Black men and had not been tried. The Monroe papers condemned the killing, and a New Orleans Democrat dispatch carried brief notices of it nationally.

episodes.title: White laborers' protest against Black workers on the New York, Ontario and Western Railroad
episodes.summary: The white laborers' protest against Black workers on the New York, Ontario and Western Railroad was a labor dispute in Orange County, New York, in August 1881, when Irish and Italian laborers grading the new line threatened to strike over reports that contractors were bringing Black workers from Maryland and the District of Columbia at $1.25 a day. New York and Chicago papers warned of a strike or riot and a protest meeting at Middletown, while correspondents writing from Middletown called the reports exaggerated. No violence was reported, and by August 9 the New-York Tribune declared the trouble over after the contractors disclaimed any present plan to bring more Black workers.

episodes.title: Shooting of an escaping prisoner in Savannah (1881)
episodes.summary: The shooting of an escaping prisoner in Savannah took place on the evening of 26 August 1881, when an officer taking an unnamed Black man to jail fired at him as he ran and hit him in the thigh. The wounded man was recaptured and returned to the jail, and the Savannah Morning News reported the incident in a brief local item the next morning.

episodes.title: Killing of Henry Cole
episodes.summary: The killing of Henry Cole was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Deputy Sheriff Cornelius of Issaquena County at Edwards, Mississippi, on a Tuesday shortly before 4 August 1881. Cornelius had come to arrest Cole and other men accused of leaving a labor contract, and after the shooting he was jailed and bound over to the Hinds County circuit court. A Mississippi paper reported that the shooting was regarded locally as "a great outrage."

episodes.title: Killing of Mack Allen
episodes.summary: The killing of Mack Allen was the fatal shooting of a Black man, named as Mack Allen or McAllen, by Jerome Pasley and a party of neighborhood men in Grayson County, Virginia, near the North Carolina line, in mid-August 1881. Allen was accused of attempting an "outrage" on a young girl, and both accounts say he was shot dead after he fired a pistol at Pasley, who was trying to take him. Both surviving accounts give the pursuers' version, and a short Virginia news paragraph about the case was reprinted in Delaware, Washington and West Virginia.

episodes.title: Beating of an unnamed Black man in Webster Parish, Louisiana (1881)
episodes.summary: The beating of an unnamed Black man in Webster Parish, Louisiana, took place in August 1881, when neighbors gave a man accused of attempting to outrage a Mrs. Crow 'a sound thrashing' and ordered him to leave the country. No death was reported, and the episode is known from a single paragraph in the Richland Beacon's column of Louisiana state news, whose editor wrote that the neighbors 'ought to have broken his neck.'

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of David Lewis
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of David Lewis took place near Elberton, Georgia, on 10 August 1881, when a crowd of Black people tried to take Lewis, a white man, from his guard after he killed a Black man named Governor Harper with a hoe. The guard fired small shot into the crowd and later dispersed it, and Lewis was afterward bound over to the Superior Court for involuntary manslaughter.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Edward Johnson
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Edward Johnson took place in Emporia, Kansas, on the evening of August 5, 1881, when a crowd of a hundred to three hundred men gathered at the Lyon county jail to hang Johnson, a Black man accused of killing Deputy Sheriff James Spillman. Johnson escaped harm because Sheriff Moon had already sent him under guard to Cottonwood Falls, and he was later committed to the asylum at Ossawatomie. The Emporia Weekly News condemned the gathering as mob law that would have disgraced the town and praised the sheriff for averting it.

episodes.title: False River ball shooting
episodes.doubt: white accounts only: Black ball-goers fired first; David Johnson's shotgun into the crowd and squads jailing 16 are part of this event
episodes.summary: The False River ball shooting was an exchange of gunfire at a Black ball on False River, Pointe Coupee Parish, Louisiana, near midnight on August 13, 1881, in which a white man, L. T. Chenvert, was killed, a white youth, Joseph Garon, was wounded, and several Black men were wounded by shotgun fire. Sixteen Black men were jailed, and two, Val Dorval and Leopold Polite, were held for murder. Every account traces to the local Pointe Coupee Banner or to brief wire dispatches, which blamed the Black men under headlines such as "Murderous Negroes."

episodes.title: Morrilton racial disturbance (1881)
episodes.summary: The Morrilton racial disturbance was a period of racial conflict in Morrilton, Arkansas, in August 1881, after a white parent beat a Black man accused of abusing white children. Street fights followed between supporters of both sides, officers swore in special police, and townspeople asked the governor for a military company. Wire reports carried it nationally as a looming "war of races," while the Conway County sheriff wrote that no such conflict was expected.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of a waiter at Mont Eagle
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of a waiter at Mont Eagle was a night attack in early August 1881 in which a mob of a dozen or more young men broke into the quarters of the Black waiters at a hotel in Mont Eagle, Tennessee, to lynch one of them. The waiter escaped when he was locked in a hotel room, and the mob's members were arrested and released on their promises not to repeat the act. The Memphis Public Ledger reported it as a "genuine sensation" under the headline "A colored Waiter That Barely Escaped Lynching."

episodes.title: Queenstown lynching threats
episodes.summary: The Queenstown lynching threats were threats in August 1881 to lynch Black suspects in the killing of two children, Joseph and Lizzie Fisher, at Queenstown in the county outside Washington, D.C. Early dispatches said men at a Washington market talked of lynching a missing Black farm hand, while the local investigation turned to an elderly Black woman, Christina Taylor, whom police later hurried to jail ahead of would-be lynchers. No lynching is reported, and the murder itself was called one of the most shocking crimes in the area in years.

episodes.title: Shooting of Cuff (Henry Brooks) at Lake City
episodes.summary: The shooting of Cuff, alias Henry Brooks, took place at Lake City, Florida, on a Wednesday afternoon in August 1881, when a deputy sheriff and a man he had summoned fired on Brooks, a Black man, as he fled arrest. A pistol ball struck him in the back of the head without serious harm, and he was captured and held under a justice's warrant.

episodes.title: Shooting of a Black man by a New Orleans policeman (1881)
episodes.summary: In August 1881 a New Orleans policeman named Reishe shot an unnamed Black man through the breast. The officer said the shooting was accidental, and a brief report in a Covington weekly added that he "will be promoted."

episodes.title: Killing of Columbus Hill
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; killed for jostling a white man
episodes.summary: The killing of Columbus Hill was the fatal stabbing of a Black bootblack by Daniel Sullivan, a white man, opposite the Hanover Market in South Baltimore, Maryland, on the night of August 20, 1881. Police arrested Sullivan within minutes while a large Black crowd followed them threatening to lynch him, and a wire report of an "apparently unprovoked and wanton" killing ran from New York to Minnesota.

episodes.title: Killing of Lovels Green and Mrs. Alguire
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; interracial relationship; date from the Aug 10 inquest report
episodes.summary: The killing of Lovels Green and Mrs. Alguire was a double homicide at Grand Haven, Michigan, on the night of about August 14, 1881, in which John Allguire shot Green, a Black man who had lived for several years with Allguire's white mother, and his mother also died. Allguire surrendered and claimed self-defence, but a coroner's jury found that he had killed both. Newspapers from New York to Virginia carried the story, stressing that the dead man was 'colored' and the woman white.

episodes.title: Killing of William Jones (Nashville, 1881)
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; quarrel began with a white man stoning a Black boy (Neal: add)
episodes.summary: The killing of William Jones was the fatal shooting of a Black man by James Ross, a white man, at Ross's house in Nashville, Tennessee, on Sunday, August 7, 1881. By the account sent over the wires, Jones had gone to ask Ross why he had hit a Black boy with a stone, and Ross answered by fetching a pistol and shooting him dead. The story ran as a short item in crime roundups across the country, while a Memphis paper printed a version in which Jones struck Ross first.

episodes.title: Killing of Henry Foster
episodes.doubt: one unknown shooter named; called out at night (night-rider pattern; may be a group)
episodes.summary: The killing of Henry Foster was the shooting of a Black farmer who was called out of his house at night near Covington, Tennessee, in August 1881 and shot dead. The assassin escaped, and the case reached newspapers only as a one-sentence wire item from Memphis.

episodes.title: Killing of Governor Harper
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; 'Wednesday of last week' before the Aug 13 report
episodes.summary: The killing of Governor Harper was the death of a Black road hand, Governor Harper, struck on the head with a hoe by a white man, David Lewis, during a quarrel near Ruckersville, Georgia, in early August 1881. Lewis was arrested, and a crowd of Black men then tried to take him from his guard to lynch him.

episodes.title: Lynching of Spence
episodes.doubt: lead from the MWT recall miss; two LoC-only state-news items and one AS item with 'lynched' OCR-garbled
episodes.summary: The lynching of Spence was the hanging of a young Black man near Frog Level, Caddo Parish, Louisiana, in mid-July 1881. Spence, said to be about 18, was accused of trying to enter a girl's room at a local house and was later found hanged. A Shreveport paper approved the killing under the heading 'Quick Justice', and the item was reprinted in Louisiana and Tennessee.

episodes.title: Lynching of Silas Lee
episodes.summary: The lynching of Silas Lee was the killing of a Black farm hand by a crowd in Lincoln parish, Louisiana, about seven miles from Vienna, in July 1881. Accused by his employer's wife of being found under her young daughter's bed, Lee was shot and left for dead, then taken out again two nights later and killed. A Baton Rouge paper printed the full account under the heading "JUDGE LYNCH" and openly approved of the killing.

episodes.title: St. Joseph exposition grounds riot (1881)
episodes.summary: The St. Joseph exposition grounds riot was an attack on Black people by a crowd of "roughs" at the exposition grounds in St. Joseph, Missouri, on July 4, 1881. The crowd tried to drive all "colored people" off the grounds, fractured one man's skull, beat a youth unconscious and fatally injured an old man named Harris before the military and extra police put down what the report called a riot.

episodes.title: Pursuit and shooting at Charles Harris near Leesburg, Georgia
episodes.summary: The pursuit and shooting at Charles Harris near Leesburg, Georgia, took place in early July 1881, when a member of a citizens' search party chased Harris, a Black railroad worker accused of assaulting a widow, and fired at him with a pistol. Harris returned fire, no one was hit, and he remained at large; the only report found, from the Albany Advertiser, called for his arrest for an "atrocious crime."

episodes.title: P Street shooting claim, Washington, 1881
episodes.doubt: unverified 'crank' story
episodes.summary: The P Street shooting claim was an account given in July 1881 by an unnamed Black man held at Police Headquarters in Washington, D.C., who said a crowd had tried to shoot him on P street for cheering for the President. No attack was confirmed, and the papers presented him as one of several "cranks" who had appeared at police headquarters.

episodes.title: Lynching of Hicks Ross
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Hicks Ross was the reported hanging of a Black prisoner by a mob that took him from the jail at Linden, Cass County, Texas, on Sunday, July 10, 1881. He had been jailed on the accusation of fatally cutting Dr. H. J. Avinger, a physician at Avinger Station on the East Line railroad. Word of the lynching came through the Dallas Herald, first as a rumor 'pretty well confirmed' and then as beyond 'little doubt'.

episodes.title: Assault on Bill Hackney
episodes.summary: The assault on Bill Hackney was an attack on a Black man during an affray between white and Black men at Columbia, Virginia, reported in early July 1881, in which he was struck on the head with a pick-handle and thrown from a window fifteen feet above the ground. The incident is known only from a one-sentence wire brief that ran in crime columns of Midwestern weeklies, which gave no cause, assailant or outcome.

episodes.title: Killing of an unidentified Black man at the Blanco River, Hays County
episodes.summary: The killing of an unidentified Black man at the Blanco River took place on July 29, 1881, when a deputy sheriff of Hays County, Texas, shot him dead near the railroad bridge over the river. The deputy was said to have fired because the man resisted arrest, and neither man's name reached the press. The killing is known from a single brief Austin dispatch whose headline called the dead man a cattle thief, a charge the dispatch itself did not make.

episodes.title: Threats against Black railroad laborers in Crawford County, Indiana
episodes.summary: In late July 1881, Black laborers hired to build the Louisville, New Albany and St. Louis railroad in Crawford County, Indiana, were threatened with exclusion from the county, and local officials refused to protect them. Reports differed on whether construction halted or the men went to work, but no violence was reported. Papers in Indianapolis, Chicago, Memphis and Savannah carried the story, the Indianapolis Leader calling it "a gross outrage" in a state "north of the Ohio river."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Henry Lawson
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Henry Lawson took place in Chattanooga, Tennessee, in July 1881, when a mob gathered at night in front of the jail where Lawson, a Black man accused of raping and cutting a young woman, was being held. According to a Chattanooga telegram dated July 11, the men were deterred by a strong sheriff's guard. Lawson was later convicted in the circuit court at Chattanooga and sentenced to hang, and the case ran as brief items in Georgia, Tennessee and Louisiana papers.

episodes.title: Burning of the Black church at Cedar Grove, Alabama
episodes.summary: The burning of the Black church at Cedar Grove, Alabama, was an arson attack on the church of a Black congregation at Cedar Grove, Bibb County, by persons described as 'white incendiaries', reported in early July 1881. According to the same report, Black incendiaries burned the white church the next night, and the pairing of the two fires was the whole of the story as it circulated in newspaper news-summary columns.

episodes.title: Fernandina disturbance of July 1881
episodes.summary: The Fernandina disturbance of July 1881 was a street conflict in Fernandina, Florida, on July 4, 1881, in which a Black man was wounded during an arrest or a quarrel with a policeman's family, and a Black crowd then threatened the men held responsible. The mayor called out the local military and the governor sent troops from Jacksonville, and a wire brief carried the story to papers from New York to Dallas as a threatened riot.

episodes.title: Killing of Henry Allen
episodes.summary: The killing of Henry Allen took place on 5 July 1881 in a harvest field near Mount Sterling, Kentucky, where a Black farm worker named Allen had his throat cut by a man named Freeman. According to a Mount Sterling dispatch, a party came to Allen's house that night to lynch him on an accusation of assaulting a woman, but found him already dead.

episodes.title: South Baltimore Fourth of July brawl (1881)
episodes.summary: The South Baltimore Fourth of July brawl was a street fight between white and Black residents of South Baltimore, Maryland, on July 4, 1881, in which a white man, William Hecker, and a Black man, Isaac Curtis, were shot. Both men were reported fatally or mortally wounded, and a Black man, Thomas H. Ross, was arrested on the charge of shooting Hecker. Papers outside Baltimore carried the case as one of a series of holiday shootings in the city.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Smith (Laurens County, Georgia)
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Smith was the shooting of a Black man by a mob in Laurens County, Georgia, reported in late July 1881. Accused of attempting the outrage of Mrs. R. T. Downing, Smith was found asleep by a pursuing mob the next day and shot to death. The episode is known only from one short paragraph printed in two Ohio newspapers under the headline "An Easy Death."

episodes.title: Posse shooting of Scott Lanier's assailant
episodes.summary: The posse shooting of Scott Lanier's assailant took place in July 1881 in the "tenth ward" of a Louisiana parish, when a constable and posse pursued and shot an unnamed Black man accused of shooting Scott Lanier. First reported as "fatally wounded," the man was described three weeks later as alive after the amputation of an arm, while Lanier had recovered.

episodes.title: Mineral Springs courthouse standoff
episodes.summary: The Mineral Springs courthouse standoff was a confrontation on July 7, 1881, at Mineral Springs, Howard County, Arkansas, between a crowd of about 200 armed Black people at a trial and armed white men of the town who turned out to protect the court officers. No one was reported hurt, but a number of Black men, including the crowd's leader, were arrested. Papers across the country carried the story as a 'Negro Riot' or a 'Race Conflict'.

episodes.title: Killing of Levi Bolden
episodes.summary: The killing of Levi Bolden took place on the morning of July 24, 1881, in the county jail at Paducah, Kentucky, where the jailer and county officials shot Bolden, a Black prisoner awaiting transfer to the penitentiary. According to the officers, Bolden had just beaten his cellmate John Stewart to death and attacked them when they opened the cell. A coroner's jury upheld the shooting the same day, and the story of the jail "tragedy" ran in papers across the country into August.

episodes.title: Killing of Jordan Thompson
episodes.summary: The killing of Jordan Thompson was the shooting of a Black man by a pursuing party near Dresden, Tennessee, after he was accused of cutting a white man on Sunday, July 31, 1881. According to the widely reprinted Dresden dispatch, officers shot him dead when he refused to surrender, while one Pennsylvania digest attributed the killing to "the avengers of Prewett." Northern and Southern papers carried the news as a brief crime item over the following week.

episodes.title: Cowan saw mill shooting
episodes.summary: The Cowan saw mill shooting was a confrontation at Cowan, Tennessee, reported in early August 1881, in which a railroad employee named Northcutt and other armed hands from his train fired on about thirty Black men gathered at a saw mill. The Black men fled and no one was reported hurt. The only known account, printed by the Winchester Home Journal as "The Cowan Affair," came from a local informant and presented the shooting as Northcutt's defense against a threatened attack.

episodes.title: Lynching of Robert Barker
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Robert Barker was the shooting of a Black prisoner by an armed group of Black men on the road from Okolona to Houston, in Chickasaw County, Mississippi, on July 30, 1881. Barker, accused of killing Luther White, a Black man, about three weeks earlier, was taken from an officer about five or six miles from Okolona, carried into the woods and shot dead. White papers headlined the case as a Black murderer "Lynched by a Mob of His Own Color," and the Okolona paper said the victim had received "a justly merited punishment."

episodes.title: Lynching of Houston Turner
episodes.summary: The lynching of Houston Turner took place on the night of July 18, 1881, in Murfreesboro, Tennessee, when a mob of about one hundred men took Turner, a nineteen-year-old Black man, from the Rutherford County sheriff and hanged him in the court-house yard. Turner had been accused of raping a white woman, Mary O'Neal, ten days earlier. The killing was reported nationally, defended by several Southern papers, and named in a reward proclamation by Governor Hawkins.

episodes.title: Lynching of Wash Allen
episodes.summary: The lynching of Wash Allen took place in DeSoto Parish, Louisiana, in July 1881, when thirty or forty masked men took Allen, a Black man jailed at Mansfield on suspicion of murdering the Kingston merchant M. J. (Judd) Scott, and hanged him at Kingston. Allen was reported to have confessed and named four or five other Black men, but a later Shreveport Times item said the confession was extorted and that the men he named proved an alibi. The hanging ran as a one-line wire item across the country, while a Mansfield correspondent wrote that local citizens approved it.

episodes.title: Lynching of Isaac Fisher
episodes.summary: The lynching of Isaac Fisher took place on Monday, July 25, 1881, when a crowd took Fisher, a Black blacksmith, from his guards at Satartia in Yazoo County, Mississippi, and hanged him from a tree outside the village. Fisher was accused of raping a young white woman and drowning her in a cistern two days earlier. Wire dispatches spread the case nationally under approving headlines.

episodes.title: Lynching of Felix Wyley
episodes.summary: The lynching of Felix Wyley was the killing of a Black prisoner by a crowd at Tiptonville, Lake County, Tennessee, on a Monday night in late July 1881. Accused of raping and murdering a young white woman, Wyley was taken from the county jail after his preliminary hearing, hanged from a tree at the edge of town and shot. The wire story ran in papers across the country, and a month later Governor Hawkins offered a $5,000 reward for members of the mob.

episodes.title: Double Horn Mob attack on the Fall Creek camp meeting
episodes.summary: The Double Horn Mob attack on the Fall Creek camp meeting was the breaking up of a Methodist campmeeting on Fall creek, Texas, by about twenty men calling themselves the "Double Horn Mob" in late July 1881. The men cut saddles and stake ropes, threw rocks, fired pistols and beat a Black man who was asleep in a wagon on the grounds. An Austin Statesman correspondent reported it as a fresh "outrage" and urged that the men, several said to be known, be punished.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Thomas Brayton
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Thomas Brayton was an armed attack by a mob on the house of a Black man at or near Paoli, Orange County, Indiana, on the night of Sunday, July 31, 1881. The defenders drove the attackers off with gunfire, and the mob withdrew carrying its wounded, with no one in the house reported hurt. An Indianapolis paper praised the armed defense as an example, while a wire brief carried the story to papers in the Dakotas and Minnesota.

episodes.title: Shooting of Jack Hicks
episodes.summary: The shooting of Jack Hicks was the wounding of a Black man by a sheriff in South Carolina in late July or on 1 August 1881, as he ran from an attempted arrest. The sheriff fired four shots and hit Hicks twice, but Hicks escaped and was reported likely to die. The only account is a paragraph from the Williamsburg Herald, reprinted on 4 August in state-news columns in Anderson and Savannah.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Smith
episodes.doubt: AP 'Saturday night' gives July 9
episodes.summary: The lynching of Henry Smith was the killing of a Black man by a mob at Des Arc, Arkansas, in July 1881, after he was accused of raping and murdering a girl of about fourteen. Some thirty or forty men took him from the town jail at night, hanged him, and threw his body into the river. Little Rock dispatches carried the story nationwide within days, and a Memphis paper defended the lynching in an editorial.

episodes.title: Death of Wilson Calder
episodes.doubt: fistfight begun by the Seabrooks after Calder's 'language'; Calder died July 3, cause disputed at the inquest
episodes.summary: The death of Wilson Calder was the death of a Black man on Edisto Island, South Carolina, on July 3, 1881, two days after he fought two white brothers, Marlon and Harry Seabrook. Black residents held that the fight killed him, a doctor found no marks of violence, and the dispute halted the inquest and left the body unburied about a week.

episodes.title: Whipping of Henry at Haynesville, Louisiana
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; whipping and order to leave over a racial 'offense'
episodes.summary: The whipping of Henry at Haynesville, Louisiana, took place on a Saturday night in mid-July 1881, when a man identified as young Mr. Smith whipped a Black boy named Henry, aged 15 or 16, and ordered him to leave. The only known account, a warning notice in an Arkansas weekly, accused Henry of entering Mrs. Smith's bedroom and urged readers to "look out for him."

episodes.title: Assault on William Tinker
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; political quarrel after the Garfield shooting
episodes.summary: The assault on William Tinker was a knife attack on a Black bootblack by Samuel Frasier, a white man from Richmond, Virginia, at the St. James Hotel corner in Washington, D.C., on Saturday, July 2, 1881. Frasier said Tinker had cursed President Garfield; the Police Court fined him $5 or 15 days.

episodes.title: Lynching of Joe Caleb
episodes.summary: The lynching of Joe Caleb took place on the night of August 31, 1881, when a party of armed men took Caleb, a young Black man held on a charge of attempting to burn a house, from the jail at Vernon in Jackson Parish, Louisiana, and hanged him beside the Trenton road. Caleb had been accused of setting fire to the house of T. J. Fuller the previous April while thirteen people were inside. An inquest failed to identify the lynchers, and a New Orleans Item editorial said it could "hardly blame" them.

episodes.title: New Hope posse shooting
episodes.summary: The New Hope posse shooting was the killing of an unnamed Black man by a bailiff named Dennis at New Hope, Georgia, on September 1, 1881, while Dennis and a posse were trying to arrest a different man. According to the wire report, the man who was shot ran out of a hut the posse had come to search and proved not to be the man they were after. Papers across the country carried the item as a short curiosity under headlines such as "Shot the Wrong Man" and "An Unlucky Negro."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Hot Springs, Arkansas (1881)
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching at Hot Springs, Arkansas, was a failed attempt by armed, masked white men to break into the Hot Springs jail on the night of September 9-10, 1881, and lynch a Black prisoner charged with attempting to outrage an elderly woman, Mrs. J. Parker. The attackers were driven off by gunfire from the jail guards and from Black men who had gathered nearby, and the accounts differed on whether anyone was hurt. A month later, dispatches reported that a Black boy supposed to be the accused, who had escaped, was found dead near Malvern and "must have" been lynched by a pursuing posse. The case drew notice because Black residents armed themselves to defend the prisoner, which a Chicago Tribune dispatch said caused "intense indignation."

episodes.title: Killing of James Hawkins
episodes.summary: The killing of James Hawkins was the fatal shooting of a Black striker by New Orleans Police Sergeant Reynolds on the morning of September 10, 1881, during a strike of the city's cotton laborers. Hawkins, a member of the Cotton Teamsters' Association, was shot during an attempted arrest of strikers who had interfered with teamsters hauling cotton. His death led the mayor to call for troops and produced a funeral that a press dispatch called the largest in the city since the war, attended by white and Black labor organizations.

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank Luck
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Frank Luck was the hanging of a Black man by a mob after he was taken from the city prison at Wortham, Texas, on a Thursday night in mid-September 1881. The news spread as a one-sentence wire item through papers in Washington, New York and Savannah. An inquest jury later could not fix the blame on anyone, which a Texas paper cited as proof that the law could not find lynchers.

episodes.title: Reported cow-carcass punishment in Morehouse Parish, Louisiana
episodes.summary: The reported cow-carcass punishment in Morehouse Parish, Louisiana, was an incident described in late summer 1881 in which unnamed men were said to have sewn a Black man accused of cow theft inside the carcass of a disemboweled cow. The story originated as a rumor in the Richland Beacon, and its location and truth were disputed by residents of the parish ward it named.

episodes.title: Atlanta Garfield memorial riot
episodes.summary: The Atlanta Garfield memorial riot was a clash on September 26, 1881, in which police, U.S. Fifth Artillery soldiers and white citizens clubbed and wounded Black people outside DeGive's Opera House in Atlanta, Georgia, during memorial services for President Garfield. Police arrested a dozen to twenty Black men, and a crowd that tried to rescue them was charged and dispersed. Papers reported it as a riot that disgraced a funeral occasion, and they disagreed on its cause and on whether anyone died.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Joe Edwards
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Joe Edwards took place in St. Louis, Missouri, on the afternoon of September 13, 1881, when a street crowd seized Edwards, a Black steamboat fireman, after he fired a pistol in a quarrel with another Black man and wounded a woman passing by. The crowd held him while men ran for a rope, but police arrived and took him to the station. Telegraph dispatches carried the story to dailies in Texas, Tennessee, Indiana and Minnesota the next day, and Midwestern weeklies reprinted it in their crime roundups.

episodes.title: Shooting at Samuel R. Hurst
episodes.summary: The shooting at Samuel R. Hurst was an attack at Laredo, Texas, in late summer 1881 in which unidentified assailants fired three or four times at Hurst, a Black man recently appointed inspector, or river guard, on the Rio Grande. He was not reported hurt, and the papers that carried the story tied the attack to his color.

episodes.title: Webb City saloon stabbings
episodes.summary: The Webb City saloon stabbings were a knife attack on two Black men, Thomas Bettes and Mack Richardson, by two white men, Berry Harwood and George Hughes, in a saloon at Webb City, Arkansas, on the night of Saturday, September 24, 1881. Bettes died within a few hours and Richardson was stabbed in the breast; Harwood was captured while Hughes escaped. A Little Rock dispatch calling it 'a horrible butchery' was reprinted across the country, and the Chicago Tribune described the killings as 'entirely unprovoked'.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Allen
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Henry Allen was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a masked mob that broke into the jail at Jacksonport, Arkansas, at about two o'clock on the morning of September 10, 1881. Allen, whom a Chicago dispatch called Henry Wallace, had been jailed on a charge of stabbing a white saloon keeper in nearby Newport. The mob overpowered the jailor and the sheriff, and Arkansas papers condemned the lynching, which a Chicago dispatch called "premature" because the wounded man recovered.

episodes.title: Savannah wharf strike shooting
episodes.summary: The Savannah wharf strike shooting was a confrontation on September 19, 1881, at the railroad bridge leading to the Central Railroad wharves in Savannah, Georgia, in which police sergeant H. H. Harvey was shot by someone in a crowd of Black striking laborers and police fired into the crowd. A squad of police with muskets then drove the strikers from the bridge, and no casualties among the crowd were confirmed. Harvey died of the wound a month later, and the strike brought out the city's militia.

episodes.title: Police shooting of Miggs Tilford
episodes.summary: The police shooting of Miggs Tilford took place at Harrodsburg, Kentucky, in September 1881 or shortly before, when policeman Meisburg shot Tilford, a Black man, during an arrest. Tilford was severely wounded, and the only known report gave as the reason that he had resisted arrest.

episodes.title: Reported lynching near Orchard Hill, Georgia
episodes.summary: The reported lynching near Orchard Hill, Georgia, was the hanging by a mob of an unnamed Black man accused of assaulting a white woman near Orchard Hill on September 12, 1881. The hanging appears in only one report, a telegraphic brief in the Washington National Republican; other printings of the same Atlanta dispatch said only that the man had been arrested and identified.

episodes.title: Lynching of Alexander Harris and Sam Bell
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Alexander Harris and Sam Bell was the shooting of two Black men by lynchers in Milam County, Texas, on a Sunday night in September 1881, while they were being taken to jail. The two men were accused of murdering W. B. Davidson, a planter they worked for, and the one known report said their bodies were "riddled with bullets."

episodes.title: Charlieville shooting (1881)
episodes.summary: The Charlieville shooting was the shooting of an unnamed Black man at Charlieville, Louisiana, on a Monday in late August 1881. He was reported to be mortally wounded, and the men who shot him were said to be still at large. The Richland Beacon, whose short item was reprinted by other Louisiana papers, treated it as the latest in a run of such shootings and demanded arrests.

episodes.title: Pocomoke City disturbance of 1881
episodes.summary: The Pocomoke City disturbance of 1881 was a confrontation between white youths and Black men in Pocomoke City, Worcester County, Maryland, beginning on Saturday evening, August 27, 1881. After a Black man was knocked down and the youths reportedly threatened to drive Black residents out, 50 or 60 Black men paraded the streets two nights later. Writs followed for 52 of the Black men, and the Snow Hill Democratic Messenger dismissed reports of a "riot" as exaggerated.

episodes.title: Savannah railroad bridge clash (1881)
episodes.summary: The Savannah railroad bridge clash was a confrontation on the morning of September 22, 1881, in Savannah, Georgia, in which police charged a crowd of Black strikers who had rushed a train bringing replacement laborers. Five Black men were wounded, none seriously according to the wire report, and one of them, Wm. Williams, was shot in the leg. The clash drew notice because a dispatch carried in Northern papers reported eight men killed, a figure the Savannah and wire accounts do not support.

episodes.title: Napier Iron Works attack
episodes.summary: The Napier Iron Works attack was a night assault in September 1881 by discharged white laborers on Black workers who had been hired in their place at the Napier Iron Works in Lawrence County, Tennessee. Accounts differed on its outcome: a Nashville report said a masked party severely beat a number of Black men, while another brief said the Black workers, who were armed, drove their attackers away. Tennessee papers described the conflict as a riot and a war between white and Black employees, and one brief called it a "race war."

episodes.title: Killing of Josephus Fairchild
episodes.summary: The killing of Josephus Fairchild took place on September 13, 1881, in Lake Charles, Louisiana, when deputy sheriffs shot a Black prisoner who broke from their custody minutes after he was sentenced to death for murder. Struck in the head by a deputy's rifle ball, he died in the parish jail that night, and a coroner's jury found the officers justified. Both Lake Charles weeklies described the escape at length, and the story ran across the country as a wire brief and as a reprinted narrative titled "A Race for Life".

episodes.title: Uniontown camp meeting shooting
episodes.summary: The Uniontown camp meeting shooting was a fight on Sunday, September 4, 1881, in which white "roughs" attacked Black attendees of a colored camp meeting near Uniontown, Fayette County, Pennsylvania. Thomas Gilbert, a Black man, was shot and thought fatally wounded, several others were shot or cut, and one Black man was chased four miles and shot in the back.

episodes.title: Hanging of Whit Brown
episodes.summary: The hanging of Whit Brown was the reported hanging, in 1881, of a Black man accused of murder by people around Red Bluff, about thirty miles below Little Rock. First rumored as a lynching, it was then described by the Russellville Democrat as a hanging done only to make Brown reveal details of the crime, and his fate was not reported.

episodes.title: Center Point riots (1881)
episodes.summary: The Center Point riots were a series of armed clashes between Black and white men at Center Point, Howard County, Arkansas, in late August 1881. Dispatches from Little Rock reported that Black men, and in one account a white man, were killed, though they disagreed on the toll. The fullest account traced one battle to the beating of a Black man, Anderson Smith, by two white men, and the story ran in weekly papers across the Midwest.

episodes.title: Lynching of Ben Robertson
episodes.summary: The lynching of Ben Robertson took place in the town of Jeanerette, Louisiana, in late September or early October 1881, when a group of armed men took Robertson, a Black man jailed on a charge of chicken stealing, out of the town jail at night, flogged him and killed him. Early reports said he was hanged, but the paper that first said so later corrected itself to say he was shot while running away. Three men were charged with his murder and held on bond, and Louisiana editors condemned the killing as mob law.

episodes.title: Lynching of Elias Robertson
episodes.summary: The lynching of Elias Robertson was the hanging of a nineteen-year-old Black man by a crowd of 300 to 400 people at Morgan's Fork, Franklin County, Mississippi, on or shortly before October 9, 1881. Robertson was accused of assaulting an elderly white widow, Mrs. Ellen Johnson, and the crowd, described as both Black and white, decided his fate by a vote before hanging him in daylight. Newspapers that carried the story stressed the vote and the crowd's mixed racial makeup, under headlines such as "Lynched by Popular Vote" and "The Voice of the Majority."

episodes.title: Shooting of Manning Law
episodes.summary: The shooting of Manning Law took place in late October 1881 near Buck Creek, South Carolina, when the two brothers of Mary Lewis, a white woman of Lexington County, overtook her and her new husband, a Black man, as the couple drove toward Augusta, Georgia. Law was shot in the breast in an exchange of pistol fire, and the brothers then hunted the preacher who had married the couple. Papers across the country carried the story as a case of "miscegenation," with conflicting reports on whether Law died.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of James Cunningham
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of James Cunningham took place on a road near Pillow's Bridge, outside Helena, Arkansas, in October 1881, when a disguised mob of about fifty men took three Black prisoners from officers and fired volleys at Cunningham. He was left for dead but was found alive the next morning, and the story of his survival ran in papers from Savannah to Minnesota.

episodes.title: Killing of Wm. Bowie
episodes.summary: The killing of Wm. Bowie was the fatal shooting of a Black steamboat roustabout by Shreveport, Louisiana, policeman E. C. McRady in late September or early October 1881, after Bowie was accused of shooting Aaron White, a Black man helping the officer make an arrest. According to the Shreveport Standard, McRady fired his rifle when Bowie advanced on him with a cocked pistol and refused to drop it. Louisiana state-news columns called Bowie a "colored desperado" and reported that McRady had been "exonerated from blame."

episodes.title: Killing of James Truss
episodes.summary: The killing of James Truss was the fatal stabbing of a Black man at Desoto, Mississippi, on a Saturday night in late September or early October 1881. Truss died within minutes of a stab wound to the neck, and five men, four white and one Black, were said to have been involved. The killing is known from a single brief in a Memphis paper's column of Mississippi news.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sandy Wright
episodes.summary: The lynching of Sandy Wright was the shooting of a Black prisoner in the jail at Blakely, Early County, Georgia, by a party of masked men in late September 1881. Wright, whose first name was also printed as "Zandy" and "Andy," was serving a sentence for hog stealing when about a dozen men forced the jailer to surrender his key and killed him in his cell. The men were not identified, and the story spread from Georgia papers to a Chicago Tribune dispatch and editorial and to short items in weeklies across the country.

episodes.title: Lynching of Edmund Davis
episodes.summary: The lynching of Edmund Davis was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd of about 300 men near Heath's store in Union County, North Carolina, on the morning of Monday, October 17, 1881. Davis, accused of raping the daughter of an aged white widow, was taken from the constable's guard escorting him to jail and hanged near the scene of the alleged crime. Papers in both Carolinas reported that about a third of the crowd was Black and that some of them urged that he be burned.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Dick Ellison
episodes.summary: The reported lynching of Dick Ellison was the death of a Black youth found dead between Hot Springs and Malvern, Arkansas, in October 1881, as reported in a dispatch dated October 14. The dispatch supposed that the dead youth was Dick Ellison, accused of attempting to outrage Mrs. Jacob Parker, and concluded that he had been caught and lynched by a pursuing posse. The item ran in at least seven newspapers within two days, but the identification and the lynching both rested on inference.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Fayette Hardee
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Fayette Hardee took place at Vaiden, Mississippi, on the night of October 7, 1881, when Hardee, a Black man, was found under the bed of a woman described as a "highly respectable young lady" and was suspected of intending to steal. According to a Dallas newspaper, a crowd "came very near lynching him," but he was not reported harmed.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jack Williams
episodes.summary: The lynching of Jack Williams took place early on October 13, 1881, when a crowd took Williams, a Black man, from the jail at Orangeburg, South Carolina, and hanged him from a tree on the edge of town. Williams had been convicted days earlier of assaulting an eleven-year-old white girl, but the jury's recommendation to mercy meant a sentence of life imprisonment instead of death. The papers stressed that the crowd overrode a completed trial, and much of the South Carolina press approved.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Redd
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of John Redd took place in October 1881 at Seale, Russell County, Alabama, when an armed crowd of several hundred tried to take Redd, a Black prisoner accused of murdering a Black woman, from the town jail. The sheriff and others persuaded the crowd to disperse, and although a wire dispatch passed on unconfirmed reports that Redd was later hanged, he was tried, found guilty of murder and sentenced to death in early November.

episodes.title: Wightman's barroom police shooting
episodes.summary: The Wightman's barroom police shooting was an incident on the night of 9 October 1881 in which a Savannah, Georgia, police officer named McDonald fired two shots at a group of Black men outside Wightman's barroom on South Broad street. No one was reported hurt by the shots and no arrest was made, and the Savannah Morning News reported the shooting in a single local brief.

episodes.title: Killing of Josephus Fairchild
episodes.summary: The killing of Josephus Fairchild took place in Lake Charles, Louisiana, shortly before October 1, 1881, when sheriff's deputies shot a Black prisoner who ran from them moments after he was sentenced to death. Struck in the head by a rifle ball, he died in the jail that night. The local Echo's account of the chase, headed "A Race for Life," was reprinted as far away as Wisconsin.

episodes.title: Sharkey County ambush of 1881
episodes.summary: The Sharkey County ambush of 1881 was the shooting of a body of Black men on their way to a Fusion political meeting in Sharkey County, Mississippi, on the night of October 28, 1881, by men hidden beside the road. Perry Thompson was killed instantly, and later accounts said two of the wounded also died. The shooters were not identified, and Mississippi papers of both parties condemned the killing as a political assassination tied to a bitter contest over county offices.

episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Jones
episodes.summary: The lynching of Charles Jones took place at Spadra, Johnson County, Arkansas, on Monday, October 31, 1881, when a mob took Jones, a Black man accused of attempting to rape a white woman, from an officer at the railroad depot and hanged him to a tree. Jones was hanged within twenty minutes of arriving at Spadra, after what the wire called a "short informal examination by a jury." A Little Rock dispatch carried the story across the country, where papers ran it under headlines such as "Speedy Justice" and "Judge Lynch's Court in Arkansas."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Boge Jackson and Henry Hill
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Boge Jackson and Henry Hill took place at Hamburg, Arkansas, on October 22, 1881, when a crowd of several thousand that had gathered to see the two Black men hanged learned that the governor had reprieved them. Many in the crowd wanted to lynch the prisoners, and one report said they were held back only with great effort, but no attack is reported. Hill's sentence was later commuted to life imprisonment, and Jackson was legally hanged at Hamburg on November 18.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bob Williams
episodes.summary: The lynching of Bob Williams was the hanging of a Black man, also reported as Robert Williams, by a crowd of about one hundred men in the woods across the Saluda River from Pelzer, South Carolina, on November 4, 1881. Williams was accused of raping a nine-year-old white girl and was taken from the guard house at Williamston. A coroner's jury found death at the hands of unknown parties, though a dispatch said the lynchers did not hide their identity and the lynching was "highly commended."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Adrian, Illinois
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching at Adrian, Illinois, took place on November 9, 1881, when a mob at Adrian, in Hancock County, tried to seize a young Black farm hand from the officers bringing him back from Peoria and shot him three times. He had been accused of assaulting a farmer's wife, Mrs. Kenkel (also spelled Kunkel), and officers carried him under guard to the county jail at Carthage, where he was reported to be dying. Short wire accounts of the shooting ran in papers from Wisconsin to Mississippi and New Mexico over the next ten days.

episodes.title: Lynching of Chris Davis
episodes.summary: The lynching of Chris Davis took place in Athens, Ohio, on the night of November 20-21, 1881, when a mob took Davis, a Black man described as a "mulatto," from the county jail and hanged him from a Hocking River bridge. Davis was being held on a charge of raping and beating with an ax an elderly widow near Albany, Ohio. A coroner's jury blamed "parties unknown," Albany women endorsed the hanging, and papers North and South debated it.

episodes.title: Lynching of Craig and Parker Jordan
episodes.summary: The lynching of Craig and Parker Jordan was the hanging of two Black men by a mob in Leflore County, Mississippi, on the night of November 26, 1881, after they were accused of assassinating Robert Catlin, a white man. Both were said to have confessed after their capture and were hanged to a tree near a place the dispatches called Shepherdstown. Wire stories carried the case across the country, and Mississippi papers greeted it as "speedy vengeance."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ed Partridge
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Ed Partridge followed the death of his six-year-old stepdaughter, Bell Holmes, on a Georgia plantation near Americus in late October or early November 1881. A coroner's jury found that the girl died of beatings at Partridge's hands, and he escaped from custody before a New York wire dispatch reported that local citizens threatened to lynch him. No lynching or recapture appears in the coverage, which spread the case nationally as a brief item under headlines such as "A Georgia Brute."

episodes.title: Caperton Station shooting
episodes.summary: The Caperton Station shooting was the shooting of a Black striking miner named Lewis by J. W. St. Clair, the prosecuting attorney of Fayette County, West Virginia, at Caperton Station on the evening of November 1, 1881. St. Clair fired on Lewis as he tried to escape after his arrest, and the first dispatches reported him killed. Later reports said he had only been wounded, and one Washington paper questioned whether he had been shot for striking or for being Black.

episodes.title: Rockdale County posse killing (1881)
episodes.summary: The Rockdale County posse killing was the fatal shooting of an unnamed Black man by a posse in Rockdale County, Georgia, reported from Atlanta on November 23, 1881. The man, accused of robbing a store, was shot dead after he refused an order to stop, and a jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide. The brief dispatch ran in papers from Georgia to Texas and Pennsylvania, which headed it variously as a robber's death or as "justifiable homicide."

episodes.title: Masked-band attacks on Black residents of Kenton, Tennessee
episodes.summary: The masked-band attacks on Black residents of Kenton, Tennessee, were a series of raids in the autumn of 1881 in which masked men repeatedly entered the Obion County town and whipped and maltreated Black men, women and children. Residents appealed to the governor, and Governor Hawkins offered a $250 reward for the arrest and conviction of those responsible. Tennessee papers carried the raids as brief state-news items, and at least one Northern paper presented them as a remnant of the Ku Klux.

episodes.title: Lynching of Massey Hill
episodes.summary: The lynching of Massey Hill took place on the night of Saturday, November 5, 1881, when a mob took Hill, a Black man, from the jail at Manchester, Tennessee, and killed him. Hill had been accused of attempting to rape a little girl near the town, and two papers reported that he was hanged. A one-sentence Nashville dispatch carried the news across the country, where it was often printed beside the lynching of Robert Williams in South Carolina the same week.

episodes.title: Killing of Robert Harvey
episodes.summary: The killing of Robert Harvey was the killing of a Black man by Sheriff Lewis of Austin County, Texas, reported in a telegram from Brenham dated November 28, 1881. The telegram said Harvey was killed while resisting arrest and described him as "a cow thief and a bad negro." The two-sentence report ran in Waco and Dallas papers and is the only account found.

episodes.title: Shooting of Manning Law
episodes.summary: The shooting of Manning Law was the pursuit and shooting of a Black man, Manning Law, by the two brothers of his white bride, Mary Lewis, in Lexington County, South Carolina, in late October 1881. Overtaken on the road soon after the wedding, Law fired at the brothers and was shot in the breast; one dispatch said he was killed, while fuller versions said he was mortally wounded and that it was not known whether he died. Papers from Illinois to Tennessee carried the story under headlines about "miscegenation", and one cited it as a case of "Judge Lynch".

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Rigney
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Charles Rigney took place at Rockville, Maryland, in November 1881, after Rigney, a young Black farm hand, was accused of assaulting the five-year-old daughter of a Montrose storekeeper. The girl's father beat him and, with four other men, bound him and delivered him to the county jail, and threats to take him out and lynch him were reported for two nights. No attack came; the grand jury indicted him for an attempt rather than rape, and papers reported that the danger of lynching had passed.

episodes.title: Whipping of Jordan Denny
episodes.summary: The whipping of Jordan Denny was a night attack on an elderly Black mail carrier at his home in Lancaster, Garrard County, Kentucky, in early November 1881, shortly before his planned wedding. Accounts disagree on the night, the attackers and his injuries, and papers in Kentucky, Texas and Utah all treated it as a comic item.

episodes.title: Killing of Felix Burke
episodes.summary: The killing of Felix Burke was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Deputy Sheriff McDonald in Monroe County, Arkansas, in early November 1881, while the deputy was trying to arrest him on a charge of stealing a mule. McDonald was badly wounded in the exchange of fire, and the episode reached distant newspapers only as a brief telegraphic crime item.

episodes.title: Marion election riot
episodes.summary: The Marion election riot was a shooting at the polls at Marion Station, Lauderdale County, Mississippi, on election day, November 8, 1881, followed that afternoon by a sheriff's posse's siege of the house of Ed Vance, a white Republican, where Black men had taken refuge. Four white men died of the shooting at the polls; at the house the posse killed Vance's son John, lost one of its own men and fired on fleeing Black men, with reports of Black dead ranging from none to fifteen. Wire reports blamed armed Black men, while Republican papers printed accounts in which white Democrats began the attack.

episodes.title: Marion election riot and Vance house siege
episodes.summary: The Marion election riot and Vance house siege was a pair of linked shootings on November 8, 1881, election day, at Marion Station in Lauderdale County, Mississippi, about five miles from Meridian. After four white men were killed or mortally wounded at the polls, a sheriff's posse of about 100 men besieged the house of Ed Vance, a white Republican, and killed his son John, while a posse member, A. G. Warren, was shot dead from the house. Wire reports blamed armed Black men and the Vances, but Republican correspondents later published a version in which white Democrats began the shooting.

episodes.title: Coal Valley strike and Black replacement miners (1881)
episodes.summary: The Coal Valley strike and Black replacement miners episode was a confrontation in November 1881 in Fayette County, West Virginia, in which striking coal miners at Coal Valley drove off the first group of Black miners brought from Virginia to take their places. When a second group arrived, county authorities called for troops, and two militia companies guarded the new men until the strikers dispersed. Accounts in the Wheeling Register differed on whether the strikers used threats: a visiting correspondent said they stopped "short of violence," while the county prosecutor said they threatened the men's lives.

episodes.title: Anniston calaboose shooting
episodes.summary: The Anniston calaboose shooting was the killing of two Black men, named in the press only as Greenwood and Hammond, by the town marshal and his deputy at the lock-up in Anniston, Alabama, in late November or early December 1881. The officers fired when a crowd of Black men pressed them as they jailed a prisoner, and an inquest and a preliminary hearing cleared them. Newspapers across the country carried the story as a riot in 'a mining town' put down by police.

episodes.title: Shooting of Hampton Price
episodes.summary: The shooting of Hampton Price was the fatal shooting of a Black man described as a "negro conjurer and so called doctor" by Oliver, the town sergeant of Franklin, Southampton County, Virginia, in December 1881. According to the reports, Price struck the officer with a black-jack when the sergeant pressed him to return fifty cents paid for a charm, and Oliver shot him in the back as he fled. Oliver was charged with the shooting, and Virginia papers took note when both witnesses for the Commonwealth died within days, leaving the prosecution without evidence.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Brodie and Shadrack Hester
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Brodie and Shadrack Hester took place in the early hours of December 1, 1881, at Oxford, Granville County, North Carolina, when a party of masked men took the two Black prisoners from the county jail and hanged them. Both men were held on a charge of murdering Thomas M. Lynch, an Oxford jeweler, and had not been tried. The Raleigh wire carried the story nationally the same day, and several North Carolina papers presented the hanging as just retribution.

episodes.title: Killing of Isaac Hicks
episodes.summary: The killing of Isaac Hicks was the fatal shooting of a Black man by two Savannah policemen at a railway section camp outside Savannah, Georgia, in late December 1881, while they were searching for a different man. Hicks ran from a shanty when the officers came to the door, was shot in three places, and died the next morning at the police barracks. The Savannah Morning News headlined the case "The Wrong Man Killed," and under a coroner's jury's majority verdict the officers were held for the grand jury.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dave Bumpers
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Dave Bumpers was the hanging of a Black eighteen-year-old by a mob at Athens, Georgia, in mid-December 1881. Bumpers had been accused of assaulting Mrs. Driscoll in her home, and the mob took him from the officers holding him and hanged him to an oak tree with a plow line. Northern and Southern papers carried the news as a short wire item, several under headlines that called him a "brute" or a "miscreant."

episodes.title: Pratt coal mines arrest shooting
episodes.summary: The Pratt coal mines arrest shooting was the killing of an unnamed Black man by an officer at the Pratt coal mines in Jefferson County, Alabama, reported in a Montgomery dispatch of December 9, 1881. According to the dispatch, the man resisted arrest and took up a shotgun, and the officer shot him before he could fire. The item ran as a brief telegraphic crime notice in papers from Pennsylvania to Texas.

episodes.title: Sibley's Mill shootings
episodes.summary: The Sibley's Mill shootings were a pair of fatal shootings in Baldwin County, Alabama, opposite Mobile, in late December 1881, in which a deputy sheriff and an unnamed Black man accused of ambushing the deputy's brother shot each other during an arrest. Deputy Sheriff Abe Johnson died within fifteen minutes, and a crowd that set out after the wounded suspect found him dead near a swamp. A Mobile dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, several of which presented the suspect's death as swift vengeance.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching at Lafayette, Alabama (1881)
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching at Lafayette, Alabama, took place in December 1881, when a crowd was reported going to the Lafayette jail to demand a Black prisoner accused of killing a merchant in Chambers County. A Montgomery dispatch said there was a "strong probability" that the man had been hanged, and papers from Savannah to Sacramento repeated the story, one of them as an accomplished lynching. No later report confirming or denying his death appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Allen
episodes.summary: The lynching of William Allen was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a party of masked men near Warwick Court House, Virginia, on the night of December 5, 1881. Allen had been jailed three days earlier, accused of fatally stabbing a white man, William S. Selater, near Newport News. The lynchers reportedly obtained him with a forged transfer order, and the one man arrested, a white barber named Thomas Valentine, was discharged for lack of evidence.

episodes.title: Disappearance and reported lynching of Mark Thompson
episodes.summary: The disappearance and reported lynching of Mark Thompson took place near Dawson, Georgia, in late November or early December 1881, when white men seized Thompson, a young Black man, as a suspect in an attack on a man named John E. Moreland and carried him away. He was reported beaten to death, but searchers found only a bloody shirt and socks buried in a swamp. A wire dispatch carried the story to papers from Pennsylvania to California, most of which headlined the robbery rather than the killing.

episodes.title: Death of an unidentified Black man near Reagan, Texas (1881)
episodes.summary: The death of an unidentified Black man near Reagan, Texas, came to light around Christmas 1881, when his body was found on a railroad track near the town after two trains had reportedly passed over it. The Waco Daily Examiner, the only paper found to report it, suggested that unknown persons had killed and robbed him and left his body on the track to hide the crime.

episodes.title: Mob hanging of Ilen Pettis
episodes.summary: The mob hanging of Ilen Pettis took place in White County, Arkansas, in late December 1881, when ten masked men took Pettis, a Black prisoner accused of robbery, from jail and hanged him from a tree limb until he confessed. The men returned him alive to the jailer and handed the recovered money to the sheriff. It is known only from one Chicago Tribune dispatch, which reported it approvingly.

episodes.title: Killing of Ed Nelms
episodes.summary: The killing of Ed Nelms was the fatal shooting of Ed Nelms, a Black man who had escaped from a Mississippi jail while under sentence of death, by Memphis Chief of Police W. C. Davis on the Arkansas bank of the Mississippi River opposite Memphis early on December 29, 1881. A coroner's jury at Memphis found the same day that Davis was "thoroughly justifiable." The Memphis dailies praised the chief at length, and a brief dispatch carried the story nationwide.

episodes.title: Lynching ruse against William Miller
episodes.summary: The lynching ruse against William Miller took place at the jail in Aberdeen, Mississippi, on the night of December 24, 1881, when Miller, a Black prisoner held as accomplice in a triple murder, was taken from his cell "under the threat and pretext of being lynched." The removal left his cellmate, the white suspect W. Robert Jones, alone to be questioned, and Jones confessed. Both men were convicted at a special term of court in January 1882 and sentenced to hang.

episodes.title: Police shooting of Sam Duckett
episodes.summary: The police shooting of Sam Duckett took place on Christmas afternoon, 25 December 1881, in South Washington, D.C., when Officer Branson shot Duckett, a Black man, in the head during a street fight over the arrest of his sister, Ellen Duckett. Duckett survived, was arrested three days later, pleaded guilty in Police Court and was fined $10 or thirty days. Washington's daily papers told the story as an attack on two policemen by a Black crowd.

episodes.title: Whipping of a Black barber in Washington, Georgia
episodes.summary: The whipping of a Black barber in Washington, Georgia, was an assault in which unnamed men took out a "negro barber" of the town, who had said he knew where Confederate gold was buried, and whipped him "nearly to death" to make him tell where it was. The Atlanta Constitution mentioned it in December 1881, in an article defending Jefferson Davis against a charge that he had misused Confederate funds.

episodes.title: Driving out of Black strikebreakers at Coal Valley, West Virginia
episodes.summary: The driving out of Black strikebreakers at Coal Valley, West Virginia, took place in late 1881, when striking coal miners in Fayette County turned back the first group of Black miners that operators had brought from Virginia to replace them. Troops were then called to guard a second group, and the Wheeling Register printed two conflicting accounts of how serious the confrontation had been.

episodes.title: Lynching of Francis Jordan
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Francis Jordan was the reported killing of a Black woman at Las Vegas, New Mexico Territory, in late 1881, for the alleged murder of a Mrs. Feste. The only known account is a one-sentence item in a Kentucky weekly, which gave no date, no description of who killed her and no circumstances.

episodes.title: Killing of John Rhodes
episodes.summary: The killing of John Rhodes was the shooting of a Black man in his cabin on the Carson place, near Friars Point, Mississippi, by two masked men on a Saturday night in late 1881, probably December 3. Rhodes died of a shot to the head, and the only report supposed that the men had meant not to kill him but to frighten him off the place.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Searcy, Arkansas (1881)
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching at Searcy was an effort by a party of men in Searcy, Arkansas, in December 1881 to hang an unnamed Black man at the urging of a visitor who offered to show the town's young men how to "hang a nigger." Before the hanging could be carried out, the lynchers were attacked by a large number of persons, and the instigator fled. The only known account is a mocking item in the Searcy Record, reprinted in the Memphis Daily Appeal.

episodes.title: Fairfax County vigilance committee expulsion (1881)
episodes.summary: The Fairfax County vigilance committee expulsion was the forced departure of an unnamed Black man from part of Fairfax County, Virginia, in early December 1881, after a newly formed vigilance committee ordered him to leave for living with a white woman. He left almost at once, and the one newspaper report of it treated the episode as a joke.

episodes.title: Shooting of Thomas Thompson
episodes.summary: The shooting of Thomas Thompson was the shooting of a Black man, described as "colored," by an officer named Griffith at Newark, Ohio, reported in December 1881. The only report found gave the officer's circumstance, that Thompson was "attempting to escape," and said nothing of whether he survived.

episodes.title: Beating of a hotel porter in Hinton, West Virginia (1881)
episodes.summary: The beating of a hotel porter in Hinton, West Virginia, was an assault on a Black porter by a man named Farris on the morning of 25 December 1881. Farris was arrested and brought before the mayor, but his friends' anger at the arresting officer led to an armed attack on the town's police the next night. Only the Richmond Dispatch's Hinton correspondent reported the beating; other papers carried only the attack on the police.

episodes.title: Hickory church burning
episodes.summary: The Hickory church burning was an attack in which a Black church at Hickory, Mississippi, was fired into and burned on a Monday night in late December 1881, and the town's calaboose was burned the same night. Three white men and a Black man were arrested on the charges, and a judge went to Hickory to investigate amid local alarm at the failure of officials to check lawlessness.

episodes.title: Burning of the Black schoolhouse at Empire, Kentucky
episodes.summary: The burning of the Black schoolhouse at Empire, Kentucky, was an arson in early June 1881 in which 'some unknown parties' set fire to a 'negro school house' at the coal-mining settlement of Empire. No one was reported hurt and no arrests were reported, but the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian called those responsible 'scoundrels' who were 'unfit to live' and urged that they be prosecuted.

episodes.title: Shooting of Will Wilkerson
episodes.summary: The shooting of Will Wilkerson took place at Malvern, Arkansas, on or about June 19, 1881, when a town marshal named Hall dangerously wounded Wilkerson, a Black man, while trying to arrest him. Wilkerson escaped to the woods and was still at large when the news was telegraphed from Little Rock the next day, with a number of people pursuing him.

episodes.title: Lynching of Josh Shorter
episodes.summary: The lynching of Josh Shorter was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd near Eufaula, Alabama, on June 9, 1881. Shorter, accused of assaulting a young white girl the day before, was captured across the river in Georgia and hanged from a tree after a crowd kept him from the sheriff. The Savannah Morning News headlined the news "Speedy Vengeance," and a brief wire item carried it to papers as far away as Utah and California.

episodes.title: Beating of William Green by Shreveport police
episodes.summary: The beating of William Green by Shreveport police took place in Shreveport, Louisiana, in mid-June 1881, when Policeman Wimbish struck Green, a Black man wanted for larceny, several times over the head with his pistol during his arrest. A crowd of Black residents gathered and threatened to free Green, and the police chief ordered the arrest of its leaders.
